---
title: "7. Databases: RDS and DynamoDB"
description: "Keeping Lemonade orders safe: a managed PostgreSQL with backups and Multi-AZ on RDS, and a key-value orders table on DynamoDB."
---

## The problem

Web servers come and go: the Auto Scaling group replaces them at will (lesson 6). The **orders** must not go with them. Running PostgreSQL yourself on EC2 means you do the backups, the security patches and the failover at 3 a.m.

We want a database that someone else keeps running, backs up every day, and can move to another AZ by itself.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip title="A librarian and a wall of lockers"}
**RDS** is like a librarian who looks after your notebook. Every night they make a copy (a backup). With Multi-AZ, they keep a **twin notebook in another building** and write every new line into both at the same time. If the first building has a fire, the twin takes over within a minute or two. You never touch the shelves: you just ask your questions at the desk (the endpoint).

**DynamoDB** is like a huge wall of **labelled lockers**. You open a locker by its exact label (the partition key), and inside, the drawers are sorted (the sort key). Opening a locker is always fast, however big the wall gets. But "which lockers contain a red ball?" means opening every locker (a scan).

Werner Vogels argues that no single database is right for every job, and that each job should use the kind of database built for it ([*A one size fits all database doesn't fit anyone*](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/2018/06/purpose-built-databases-in-aws.html), 2018). DynamoDB grew out of the ideas in Amazon's famous [*Dynamo* paper](https://www.allthingsdistributed.com/files/amazon-dynamo-sosp2007.pdf) (DeCandia et al., 2007), written after Amazon's shopping cart needed to stay writable even while servers failed.
:::

## The concept, precisely

**Amazon RDS** (Relational Database Service) runs PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, Oracle, SQL Server or Db2 for you.

- A **DB instance** has an **instance class** (for example `db.t4g.micro`) and **storage** (for example 20 GB of gp3).
- A **DB subnet group** lists private subnets in at least two AZs that the database may use.
- The **endpoint** is a DNS name such as `lemonade-db.abc123.eu-west-2.rds.amazonaws.com`. Apps connect to it, never to an IP address.
- **Automated backups** take a daily snapshot and keep transaction logs, so you can restore to **any second** in the retention period (1–35 days). RDS uploads the logs every 5 minutes.
- **Multi-AZ** keeps a **synchronous standby** in another AZ. If the primary fails, RDS points the endpoint at the standby. This typically takes 60–120 seconds.
- **Read replicas** are asynchronous copies for extra read traffic. They are not a backup.
- A **managed master password** (`--manage-master-user-password`) is stored and rotated in AWS Secrets Manager, so it never appears in your scripts.

**Amazon DynamoDB** is a serverless key-value and document database.

- A **table** holds **items** (up to 400 KB each) made of **attributes**.
- The **primary key** is a **partition key**, optionally plus a **sort key**. For orders: partition key `order_date`, sort key `order_id`.
- **Query** reads all items with one partition key, in sort-key order, which is fast. **Scan** reads the whole table, which is slow and costly.
- **Capacity modes**: **on-demand** (pay per request, nothing to plan) or **provisioned** (you reserve read and write units per second).
- Reads are **eventually consistent** by default (half price), or **strongly consistent** if you ask.

| Command or option | What it does | Rule / convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `aws rds create-db-subnet-group` | where the database may live | private subnets in 2+ AZs | `--db-subnet-group-name lemonade-db --subnet-ids subnet-a subnet-b` |
| `aws rds create-db-instance` | creates the database | the options below | `--db-instance-identifier lemonade-db --engine postgres` |
| `--db-instance-class` | size | start with a burstable class | `--db-instance-class db.t4g.micro` |
| `--allocated-storage` | disk size in GB | can grow later, never shrink | `--allocated-storage 20` |
| `--manage-master-user-password` | password in Secrets Manager | never put passwords on the command line | `--master-username lemonade --manage-master-user-password` |
| `--multi-az` | synchronous standby in another AZ | on for production, off for practice | `--multi-az` |
| `--backup-retention-period` | days of point-in-time restore | the API default is 1; set it explicitly | `--backup-retention-period 7` |
| `--no-publicly-accessible` | no public IP | databases stay private | `--no-publicly-accessible` |
| `aws rds describe-db-instances` | status and endpoint | wait for `available` | `--query 'DBInstances[].Endpoint.Address'` |
| `aws rds restore-db-instance-to-point-in-time` | restores to a second in the past | creates a **new** instance | `--restore-time 2026-11-25T09:00:00Z` |
| `aws rds delete-db-instance` | deletes it | keep a final snapshot of real data | `--final-db-snapshot-identifier lemonade-final` |
| `aws dynamodb create-table` | creates a table | define only key attributes | `--key-schema AttributeName=order_date,KeyType=HASH ...` |
| `aws dynamodb put-item` / `get-item` | write / read one item | values are typed: `S`, `N`, `BOOL`, `M`, `L` | `--item '{"order_id":{"S":"0001"}}'` |
| `aws dynamodb query` | items of one partition | needs the partition key | `--key-condition-expression "order_date = :d"` |
| `aws dynamodb scan` | reads everything | avoid on big tables | `scan --table-name lemonade-orders` |

## Worked example: the orders database

The PostgreSQL database for the stand:

```bash
aws rds create-db-instance --db-instance-identifier lemonade-db \
  --engine postgres --db-instance-class db.t4g.micro --allocated-storage 20 \
  --master-username lemonade --manage-master-user-password \
  --db-subnet-group-name lemonade-db --vpc-security-group-ids "$DB_SG" \
  --backup-retention-period 7 --no-publicly-accessible
aws rds describe-db-instances --db-instance-identifier lemonade-db \
  --query 'DBInstances[].[DBInstanceStatus,Endpoint.Address]' --output text
```

Illustrative output a few minutes later (RDS is not in LocalStack's free edition):

```text
available	lemonade-db.c1a2b3c4d5e6.eu-west-2.rds.amazonaws.com
```

The same orders as a DynamoDB table, one order and one query, from [`examples/localstack-demo.sh`](examples/localstack-demo.sh):

```bash
aws dynamodb create-table --table-name lemonade-orders --billing-mode PAY_PER_REQUEST \
  --attribute-definitions AttributeName=order_date,AttributeType=S AttributeName=order_id,AttributeType=S \
  --key-schema AttributeName=order_date,KeyType=HASH AttributeName=order_id,KeyType=RANGE \
  --query TableDescription.TableStatus --output text
aws dynamodb put-item --table-name lemonade-orders \
  --item '{"order_date":{"S":"2026-11-25"},"order_id":{"S":"0001"},"cups":{"N":"2"}}'
aws dynamodb query --table-name lemonade-orders --key-condition-expression "order_date = :d" \
  --expression-attribute-values '{":d":{"S":"2026-11-25"}}' --query Count
```

Output (LocalStack): the table status `ACTIVE`, then the number of orders on 25 November:

```text
ACTIVE
1
```

## Rules and conventions

- **Databases live in private subnets.** Their security group allows port 5432 only from the web servers' security group.
- **Turn on backups and test a restore.** A backup you have never restored is a hope, not a plan.
- **Multi-AZ for anything customers depend on.** It doubles the instance price and removes the single point of failure.
- **Connect by endpoint name**, never by IP, so a failover just works.
- **Design DynamoDB keys from your questions.** First write down how you will read the data ("orders of one day"), then choose the keys so that each question is a Query.
- **Delete practice databases** after the lesson, with `--skip-final-snapshot` only if the data truly does not matter.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `--publicly-accessible` with `0.0.0.0/0` on 5432 | bots try passwords all day | private subnets; allow only the web security group |
| Read replica treated as a backup | a bad `DELETE` is copied to the replica too | use point-in-time restore or snapshots |
| Backup retention left at 1 day | the mistake from last week cannot be undone | `--backup-retention-period 7` or more |
| DynamoDB `scan` in the web page | slow pages and a growing bill | add a key or an index so a Query answers the question |
| One "hot" partition key for everything | throttling at busy times | spread writes over many key values (for example per day *and* per stand) |

## Mathematical Abstraction

How much data can a failure lose? If orders arrive at a steady rate, the loss is at most

$$
L = \lambda \cdot \text{RPO}
$$

where:

- $L$ is the number of orders that could be lost;
- $\lambda$ (lambda) is the arrival rate, in orders per minute;
- $\text{RPO}$ (recovery point objective) is how far back the newest safe copy can be, in minutes.

Example: on a busy Saturday $\lambda = 30$ orders per hour $= 0.5$ per minute. Restoring from backups alone (logs every 5 minutes, so $\text{RPO} \le 5$) can lose up to $L = 0.5 \times 5 = 2.5$, so at most 3 orders. With Multi-AZ the standby is written synchronously, so for a lost primary $\text{RPO} = 0$ and $L = 0.5 \times 0 = 0$. The customers wait 60–120 seconds during the failover, but no order disappears.

DynamoDB counts work in **units**. For an item of size $s$ kilobytes:

$$
w = \left\lceil \frac{s}{1} \right\rceil, \qquad
r_{\text{strong}} = \left\lceil \frac{s}{4} \right\rceil, \qquad
r_{\text{eventual}} = \frac{1}{2} \left\lceil \frac{s}{4} \right\rceil
$$

where:

- $s$ is the item size in KB;
- $w$ is the write units for one write, charged per started 1 KB;
- $r_{\text{strong}}$ is the read units for one strongly consistent read, per started 4 KB;
- $r_{\text{eventual}}$ is the read units for one eventually consistent read, half as much;
- $\lceil \cdot \rceil$ rounds up, because a started block counts as a whole one.

Example: one Lemonade order item is $s = 1.5$ KB. A write costs $w = \lceil 1.5 \rceil = 2$ units. A strong read costs $\lceil 1.5/4 \rceil = \lceil 0.375 \rceil = 1$ unit, and an eventual read $0.5$ units.

The on-demand monthly bill is then

$$
C = W \cdot w \cdot p_w + R \cdot r \cdot p_r
$$

where:

- $C$ is the monthly cost in dollars;
- $W$ and $R$ are the numbers of writes and reads in the month;
- $w$ and $r$ are the units per write and per read from the formula above;
- $p_w$ and $p_r$ are the prices per unit: in London \$0.7423 and \$0.1487 per **million** units (price at time of writing, November 2026).

Example: 100,000 orders written once and read twice (eventually consistent) in a month gives $W = 100{,}000$, $w = 2$, $R = 200{,}000$, $r = 0.5$. So $C = 100{,}000 \times 2 \times 0.7423 \times 10^{-6} + 200{,}000 \times 0.5 \times 0.1487 \times 10^{-6} = 0.1485 + 0.0149 \approx \$0.16$. The first 25 GB of storage are free, so a small stand pays almost nothing.
